prompt: Shareholders invest 50,000 in cash in a new company in exchange for ordinary shares. Record the entry.

reasoning: An asset (cash) increases: debit.
Equity contributed by owners increases: credit share capital.
No revenue is earned, so the income statement is untouched.

why_it_matters: Equity raised is financing, not performance. Separating contributed capital from earned profit is how you judge whether a company funds itself.
common_trap: Crediting revenue. Money from owners is never income.

prompt: The company buys equipment for 18,000 on 30-day credit terms. Record the entry.

reasoning: The equipment is an asset: debit.
An obligation to the supplier arises: credit trade payables.
Capex appears in investing cash flow only when it is paid.

why_it_matters: Capex bought on credit shows up in investing cash flow later than on the balance sheet. Check the non-cash investing note when capex and PP&E growth don't match.
common_trap: Expensing equipment, or recording a cash outflow on the day of purchase.

prompt: A consulting firm completes work worth 7,500 for a client and invoices it, payable in 30 days. Record the entry.

reasoning: The work is done, so revenue is earned now (accrual basis).
The right to be paid is an asset: debit trade receivables.

why_it_matters: Revenue without cash raises receivables and DSO. Profit and operating cash flow diverge until the client pays.
common_trap: Waiting for cash before recording revenue.

prompt: A customer pays 4,000 of an invoice already recorded as a receivable. Record the entry.

reasoning: One asset (cash) up, another (receivable) down.
Revenue was recognised when the work was done, so no revenue now.

why_it_matters: Collections convert profit into cash. Strong collection lowers working capital and lifts operating cash flow without touching profit.
common_trap: Crediting revenue a second time.

prompt: On 1 November the company pays 2,400 for a 12-month insurance policy starting that day. Record the payment.

reasoning: The cover has not been used yet, so the payment buys an asset (a prepayment).
It becomes an expense month by month.

why_it_matters: Prepayments move cash out before the expense hits profit. Growing prepayments can depress CFO while profit is unaffected.
common_trap: Expensing the full 2,400 immediately.

prompt: The 2,400 twelve-month policy paid on 1 November is still recorded as a prepayment. Record the adjusting entry at 31 December.

reasoning: Monthly cost = 2,400 / 12 = 200.
Two months used (Nov, Dec): 400 moves from the asset to expense.
Remaining prepayment: 2,000 for 10 months.

why_it_matters: Adjusting entries match costs to the period that consumed them. Without them, profit swings with payment dates instead of activity.
common_trap: Crediting cash. The cash moved in November; the adjustment never touches cash.

prompt: On 1 October a client pays 12,000 in advance for 12 months of service, recorded as unearned revenue. Record the adjusting entry at year end, 31 December.

reasoning: Revenue is recognised as the service is performed, not when cash arrives.
3 of 12 months are done: 12,000 × 3/12 = 3,000 moves from the liability to revenue.

why_it_matters: Growing unearned revenue is cash collected before profit: a sign of customer demand and a working-capital advantage.
common_trap: Debiting cash at year end. The cash entry was made on 1 October.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IFRS 15 calls this a contract liability; the label 'unearned revenue' is still allowed.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 606 is converged with IFRS 15 here; same timing and the same contract-liability concept.

prompt: Equipment costing 18,000 was bought on 1 July. Useful life 5 years, no residual value, straight-line. Record depreciation for the year to 31 December.

reasoning: Annual charge = 18,000 / 5 = 3,600.
Six months in use: 3,600 × 6/12 = 1,800.
Credit the contra-asset so the original cost stays visible.

why_it_matters: Depreciation is non-cash but real: it is the cost of the capacity used. Comparing depreciation with capex shows whether the asset base is being renewed.
common_trap: Charging a full year for an asset held six months, or crediting the equipment account directly.

prompt: Staff earn 5,000 per five-day week, paid every Friday. The year ends on a Wednesday. Record the accrual for the unpaid days.

reasoning: Monday to Wednesday worked but unpaid: 3 days = 3,000.
Expense now; liability until payday.

why_it_matters: Accrued liabilities let profit reflect costs actually incurred. Unusual falls in accruals can flatter operating cash flow or hide unrecorded costs.
common_trap: Accruing the whole week (5,000), or nothing because no cash was paid.

prompt: A 20,000 note payable at 6% a year was signed on 1 September; interest is due at maturity. Record the interest accrual at 31 December.

reasoning: Annual interest = 20,000 × 6% = 1,200.
Four months (Sep–Dec): 1,200 × 4/12 = 400.

why_it_matters: Interest accrues with time whether or not it is paid. Unrecorded accrued interest understates both leverage and finance cost.
common_trap: Counting three months (forgetting September) or adding interest to the note's principal.

prompt: In December the firm completed 1,500 of work that will be invoiced in January; it already has an unconditional right to be paid. Record the year-end accrual.

reasoning: Revenue belongs to the period in which the work was done.
An unconditional right to consideration is a receivable; if the right still depended on further performance it would be a contract asset.

why_it_matters: Accrued and unbilled revenue relies on judgement. Rapid growth in unbilled amounts relative to revenue is a classic earnings-quality warning.
common_trap: Leaving the revenue for January because the invoice is issued then.

ifrs_gaap.ifrs: IFRS 15: receivable if the right to payment is unconditional (only time must pass); otherwise a contract asset.
ifrs_gaap.us_gaap: ASC 606 uses the same receivable vs contract-asset split; the book's US examples call it accounts receivable.

prompt: Supplies on hand were 1,200 at the start of the year and 800 more were bought (recorded as an asset). A count at year end finds 300. Record the adjustment.
why_it_matters: Physical counts anchor the books to reality. Skipped counts are a common route to overstated assets.
common_trap: Expensing only the 800 bought this year, or expensing the 300 left.

prompt: During the year the company declared dividends of 2,000, recorded in a separate dividends account. Record the closing entry for that account at year end.

reasoning: Dividends are a temporary account that reduces equity; it is not an expense.
Closing transfers its balance to retained earnings and resets it to zero for next year.

why_it_matters: Distributions come out of retained earnings, never profit. Confusing the two overstates the payout capacity you think a company has.
common_trap: Closing dividends to the income summary as if they were an expense.

prompt: Debit and credit rules

answer.meaning: Debits increase assets, expenses and dividends; credits increase liabilities, equity and income.
answer.formula: Assets = Liabilities + Equity; Equity = contributed capital + retained earnings (income − expenses − dividends)
answer.interpretation: Every entry keeps the equation balanced: total debits = total credits.
answer.high_signals: A large debit balance in an income account (or credit in an asset) usually signals an error.

why_it_matters: Reading a trial balance fast is the first step of any due-diligence or audit review.
common_trap: Thinking 'debit' means good or 'credit' means bad. They are just sides.

prompt: What is the normal balance of unearned revenue?
options: Credit, because it is a liability
Debit, because it is revenue
Debit, because it is an asset
It has no normal balance

reasoning: Unearned revenue is an obligation to deliver service: a liability.
Liabilities increase with credits.

why_it_matters: Classifying advance payments correctly keeps revenue honest and shows customer-funded working capital.
common_trap: Treating it as revenue because of its name.

prompt: Which statement about year-end adjusting entries is true?
options: They always involve one income statement account and one balance sheet account, and never cash
They always involve cash
They only affect the balance sheet
They are needed only under cash-basis accounting

reasoning: Adjustments align revenue and expense with the period (accruals and deferrals).
Cash movements were already recorded when they happened.

why_it_matters: Knowing adjustments never touch cash lets you separate timing effects from real cash generation.
common_trap: Crediting cash in an accrual adjustment.

prompt: Which error would NOT be revealed by a trial balance that balances?
options: A purchase of supplies debited to equipment instead of supplies
A debit of 450 posted as 540 with the credit posted correctly
A debit posted but the related credit omitted
A credit balance listed in the debit column

reasoning: Posting to the wrong account on the correct side keeps debits equal to credits.
The other errors make the columns disagree.

why_it_matters: A balanced trial balance proves arithmetic, not correctness. Misclassification (expense as asset) is exactly how profit gets overstated.
common_trap: Assuming a balancing trial balance means the books are right.

prompt: Cash received from customers 80,000. Trade receivables rose by 6,000 and unearned revenue rose by 2,000. Accrual-basis revenue?

reasoning: Add the increase in receivables (earned, not yet collected).
Deduct the increase in unearned revenue (collected, not yet earned).

why_it_matters: Converting cash to accruals is the reverse of the indirect cash flow statement. Both directions must be automatic.
common_trap: Adding the increase in unearned revenue.

book_ref.section: Conversion from Cash Basis to Accrual Basis

prompt: Rent of 3,600 for 12 months was paid on 1 April. Rent expense for the year to 31 December?

reasoning: 300 per month × 9 months (Apr–Dec) = 2,700
Prepayment left: 900
explanation.shortcut: Monthly amount first, then months elapsed.

why_it_matters: Time-apportioning is behind every accrual and deferral.
common_trap: Counting 8 months (forgetting April).

prompt: Accruals vs deferrals

answer.meaning: Accruals record revenue or expense before cash moves; deferrals record cash before the revenue or expense is earned or incurred.
answer.formula: Accruals: accrued revenue (asset) / accrued expense (liability). Deferrals: prepaid expense (asset) / unearned revenue (liability).
answer.interpretation: Both make profit reflect the period's activity rather than its cash timing.
answer.high_signals: Large accruals: more estimates, more room for error or management.
answer.low_signals: Profit close to cash; simpler business.

why_it_matters: The gap between profit and CFO is made of exactly these items.
common_trap: Mixing up prepaid expenses (asset) and accrued expenses (liability).

prompt: A company forgets to accrue 3,000 of wages earned at year end. What is the effect on the year's statements?
options: Expenses and liabilities understated by 3,000; net income and equity overstated by 3,000; assets unaffected
Assets overstated by 3,000
Net income understated by 3,000
No effect, because the wages are paid next year

reasoning: The missing entry is Dr wages expense / Cr wages payable.
So expense and liability are both too low; profit and retained earnings too high.
No asset is involved.

why_it_matters: Missed accruals flatter this year's profit and hit next year's. Watch for profits that jump while accrued liabilities fall.
common_trap: Thinking an unpaid cost has no effect until it is paid.

prompt: Which account is NOT closed at year end?
options: Unearned revenue
Service revenue
Salaries and wages expense
Dividends declared

reasoning: Temporary accounts (income, expenses, dividends) are closed to retained earnings.
Balance sheet accounts such as unearned revenue carry forward.

why_it_matters: Knowing what carries forward tells you what next year's statements start with.
common_trap: Closing a liability because the word 'revenue' is in its name.

prompt: Closing entries

answer.meaning: Entries that transfer the balances of temporary accounts (income, expenses, dividends) to retained earnings, resetting them to zero.
answer.formula: Closing RE = Opening RE + Income − Expenses − Dividends
answer.interpretation: After closing, only balance sheet accounts remain (post-closing trial balance).

why_it_matters: It is the bookkeeping version of the retained-earnings roll-forward you use in every three-statement model.
common_trap: Thinking closing entries change total equity. They only move amounts within it.

prompt: What does a reversing entry do, why is it optional, and when is it useful?

answer.model_answer: A reversing entry is made on the first day of the new period and is the exact opposite of a year-end accrual adjustment (for example, Dr wages payable / Cr wages expense). It is optional because it does not change the financial statements: the totals end up the same with or without it. Its value is practical: when the cash is later paid, the clerk can record the whole payment routinely as an expense without splitting it between the old liability and the new expense, which reduces errors.
rubric: Opposite of the accrual on day one
Simplifies recording of the later payment

reasoning: Reverse the accrual, then record the full payment as expense; the net expense in the new year is only the new-year portion.

why_it_matters: Understanding that bookkeeping shortcuts don't change economics helps you focus on what actually moves the numbers.
common_trap: Thinking reversing entries are compulsory or that they change net income.

prompt: A small business reports on a cash basis. Its owner says profit jumped 40% this year. What should you check first?
options: Whether customers paid old invoices early or suppliers were paid late, which shifts cash-basis profit between years
The depreciation method
The tax rate
Whether the business uses FIFO

reasoning: Cash-basis profit follows payment timing, not activity.
Collecting last year's receivables or delaying payments inflates this year's figure.
Convert to accruals using the change in receivables, payables, prepayments and accruals.

why_it_matters: When buying a small company, always convert cash-basis figures to accruals before valuing it.
common_trap: Valuing a business on a cash-basis profit spike.

book_ref.section: Theoretical Weaknesses of the Cash Basis
